arXiv:1908.03428v2 [math.PR] 07 Jun 2023

On some new moments of Gamma type

Tetyana Kadankova Address: Vakgroep Wiskunde, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Gebauw G, Pleinlaan 2, 1050 Elsene, Belgium. Email: tetyana.kadankova@vub.be , Thomas Simon Address: Laboratoire Paul Painlevé, Université de Lille, Cité Scientifique, 59655 Villeneuve d’Ascq Cedex, France. Email: thomas.simon@univ-lille.fr and Min Wang Address: Jingzhai 301, Yau Mathematical Sciences Center, Tsinghua University, Haidian District, Beijing 100084, China. Email: minwangmath@tsinghua.edu.cn
Abstract.

We investigate certain positive random variables having moments of Gamma type. Some necessary and some sufficient conditions are given for their existence. In particular, we observe that the Weber-Schafheitlin formula for the Bessel function makes it possible to construct non-trivial moments of Gamma type having a signed spectral measure.

Key words and phrases: 
Bessel function; Meijer GG-function; Moment of Gamma type; Quasi-infinite divisibility
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
33C10; 33C20; 60E07; 60E10

1. Introduction and statement of the results

1.1. The general setting

Introduce the notation

(𝐚)s=(a1)s×⋯×(an)s=∏i=1nΓ⁡(ai+s)Γ⁡(ai)({\bf a})_{s}\;=\;(a_{1})_{s}\,\times\,\cdots\,\times\,(a_{n})_{s}\;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{{\Gamma}(a_{i}+s)}{{\Gamma}(a_{i})}

for 𝐚={a1,…,an}{\bf a}=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\} with 0<a1≤…≤an0<a_{1}\leq\ldots\leq a_{n} and s>−a1,s>-a_{1}, where we have used the standard definition of the Pochhammer symbol (x)s(x)_{s} built on the Gamma function Γ⁡(z),z>0.\Gamma(z),z>0. When n=0n=0 that is 𝐚{\bf a} is empty, we set min⁡(𝐚)=∞\min({\bf a})=\infty and (𝐚)s=1.({\bf a})_{s}=1. In [3], the authors introduce the notation

D⁡[𝐚𝐛𝐜𝐝]{\rm D}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}{\bf a}&{\bf b}\\ {\bf c}&{\bf d}\end{array}\right]

for the distribution of the positive random variable X,X, if it exists, such that

(1) 𝔼⁡[Xs]=(𝐚)s​(𝐛)−s(𝐜)s​(𝐝)−s{\mathbb{E}}[X^{s}]\;=\;\frac{({\bf a})_{s}({\bf b})_{-s}}{({\bf c})_{s}({\bf d})_{-s}}

for every s∈(−min⁡(𝐚),min⁡(𝐛)),s\in(-\min({\bf a}),\min({\bf b})), where 𝐚,𝐛,𝐜{\bf a},{\bf b},{\bf c} and 𝐝{\bf d} are four finite and possibly empty sets of positive numbers. A challenging open problem is to characterize the existence of such distributions in terms of the four finite sets 𝐚,𝐛,𝐜{\bf a},{\bf b},{\bf c} and 𝐝.{\bf d}.

When they exist, these distributions are unique by uniqueness of the Mellin transform on the non-trivial strip (−min⁡(𝐚),min⁡(𝐛)).(-\min({\bf a}),\min({\bf b})). From the point of view of special functions, the Mellin transform is also formerly invertible in a Meijer G−G-function. More precisely, one has by definition

(2) ∫0∞f⁡(x)​xs−1​𝑑x=(𝐚)s​(𝐛)−s(𝐜)s​(𝐝)−s\int_{0}^{\infty}f(x)\,x^{s-1}\,dx\;=\;\frac{({\bf a})_{s}({\bf b})_{-s}}{({\bf c})_{s}({\bf d})_{-s}}

for every s∈(−min⁡(𝐚),min⁡(𝐛)),s\in(-\min({\bf a}),\min({\bf b})), where ff is the Meijer G−G-function

f(x)=Gp+n,q+mm,n(x−1|𝐀𝐁)f(x)\;=\;G^{m,n}_{p+n,q+m}\left(x^{-1}\left|\begin{array}[]{c}{\bf A}\\ {\bf B}\end{array}\right.\right)

with 𝐀={1−an,…,1−a1,d1,…,dp}{\bf A}=\{1-a_{n},\ldots,1-a_{1},d_{1},\ldots,d_{p}\} and 𝐁={b1,…,bm,1−cq,…,1−c1}{\bf B}=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{m},1-c_{q},\ldots,1-c_{1}\} finite and possibly empty sets. We refer to Chapter 16 in [13] for more detail on the Meijer G−G-functions. One should remember that the above ff is a function strictly speaking on (0,1)∪(1,∞)(0,1)\cup(1,\infty) only, and that there might be a singularity at one. For example, if 𝐚=(1,3),𝐜=(2,2){\bf a}=(1,3),{\bf c}=(2,2) and 𝐛=𝐝=∅,{\bf b}={\bf d}=\emptyset, an easy computation shows that the corresponding random variable XX exists with distribution

ℙ[X∈dx]=12(δ1(dx)+ 1(0,1)dx).{\mathbb{P}}[X\in dx]\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\,(\delta_{1}(dx)\,+\,{\bf 1}_{(0,1)}\,dx).

The solution to the above existence problem amounts to characterizing the non-negativity of ff on (0,1)∪(1,∞)(0,1)\cup(1,\infty) and of the singularity at one. To this end, simulations of Meijer G−G-functions can be performed by the Wolfram package [16], which is however not very robust when the amount of parameters becomes large or in the presence of the singularity. The general problem of the non-negativity of Meijer functions on the positive half-line is a hard one, which can be traced back to [11] for the classical hypergeometric function.

1.2. The case 𝐛=∅{\bf b}=\emptyset

Before stating, in the next paragraph, our contribution to this problem, let us give an account on the case 𝐛=∅,{\bf b}=\emptyset, which has been studied in [3, 6, 7, 9] from various points of view. It is clear that the condition 𝐝=∅{\bf d}=\emptyset is then necessary for the existence of X.X. Moreover, considering the random variable X−1,X^{-1}, the problem is equivalent to the case 𝐚=𝐜=∅.{\bf a}={\bf c}=\emptyset. Here and throughout, 𝚪t{\bf\Gamma}_{t} denotes a standard Gamma random variable with parameter t>0t>0 and we make the convention that an empty product is one. When p≥1,p\geq 1, the following necessary conditions for the existence of XX are obtained in [3]:

(3) {p≤n,a1≤c1,a1+⋯+ap≤c1+⋯+cp.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}p\,\leq\,n,\\ a_{1}\,\leq\,c_{1},\\ a_{1}+\cdots+a_{p}\,\leq\,c_{1}+\cdots+c_{p}.\end{array}\right.

This set of conditions is easily seen to be sufficient for p=1p=1 or n=2.n=2. For p=1p=1 one has indeed

X=d𝐁a1,c1−a1×𝚪a2×⋯×𝚪anX\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf B}_{a_{1},c_{1}-a_{1}}\,\times\,{\bf\Gamma}_{a_{2}}\,\times\,\cdots\,\times\,{\bf\Gamma}_{a_{n}}

where 𝐁a,b{\bf B}_{a,b} denotes, here and throughout, a standard Beta random variable with parameter a,b>0a,b>0 and we make the conventions 𝐁0,b=0{\bf B}_{0,b}=0 for all b>0b>0 and 𝐁a,0=1{\bf B}_{a,0}=1 for all a>0.a>0. It is interesting to mention that for n=2,n=2, an example of such independent Beta-Gamma products is the square of a Brownian supremum area, which is thoroughly studied in [7] - see Theorem 1.6 therein. To show the sufficiency of (3) in the remaining case p=n=2,p=n=2, we first write down the general formula

(4) (𝐚)s(𝐜)s=exp−{∫0∞(1−e−s​x)​(φ𝐚​(x)−φ𝐜​(x)x⁡(1−e−x))​𝑑x}\frac{({\bf a})_{s}}{({\bf c})_{s}}\;=\;\exp-\left\{\int^{\infty}_{0}(1-e^{-sx})\left(\frac{\varphi_{\bf a}(x)-\varphi_{\bf c}(x)}{x(1-e^{-x})}\right)\,dx\right\}

1.3. A family of solutions for 𝐚≠∅{\bf a}\neq\emptyset and 𝐛≠∅{\bf b}\neq\emptyset

We now come back to the general setting of Paragraph 1.1, and we use the notations therein. By the same arguments as in [3], the following conditions are easily seen to be necessary:

{p+q≤n+m,min⁡(𝐚)≤min⁡(𝐜),min⁡(𝐛)≤min⁡(𝐝).\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}p+q\,\leq\,n+m,\\ \min({\bf a})\,\leq\,\min({\bf c}),\\ \min({\bf b})\,\leq\,\min({\bf d}).\end{array}\right.

Moreover, in the case p=q=1p=q=1 these conditions are also sufficient, with

X=d𝐁a1,c1−a1×𝚪a2×⋯×𝚪an𝐁b1,d1−b1×𝚪b2×⋯×𝚪bm⋅X\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\frac{{\bf B}_{a_{1},c_{1}-a_{1}}\,\times\,{\bf\Gamma}_{a_{2}}\,\times\,\cdots\,\times\,{\bf\Gamma}_{a_{n}}}{{\bf B}_{b_{1},d_{1}-b_{1}}\,\times\,{\bf\Gamma}_{b_{2}}\,\times\,\cdots\,\times\,{\bf\Gamma}_{b_{m}}}\cdot

The following theorem shows however that the condition p≤np\leq n which was necessary in the setting of the previous paragraph, is in general not necessary anymore.

defined for all α∈ℝ\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}} and z∈ℂ/ℝ−.z\in{\mathbb{C}}/\penalty{\mathbb{R}}^{-}. A short new proof of the latter formula is given in the Appendix for the sake of completeness. 2.2. Proof of Theorem 2

Proof.

Fix a,b>0a,b>0 and consider

𝒟a,b={(c,d)∈(a,∞)×(a,∞)such thatD[ab(c,d)−]exists}.{\mathcal{D}}_{a,b}\;=\;\left\{(c,d)\in(a,\infty)\times(a,\infty)\;\mbox{such that}\;{\rm D}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}a&b\\ (c,d)&-\end{array}\right]\;\mbox{exists}\right\}.

It is clear from the definition that the set 𝒟a,b{\mathcal{D}}_{a,b} is closed and symmetric with respect to the line {c=d}.\{c=d\}. Theorem 1 shows that 𝒟t,a,b=𝒟a,b∩{c+d=t}{\mathcal{D}}_{t,a,b}={\mathcal{D}}_{a,b}\cap\{c+d=t\} is non-empty if and only if t≥3​a+b+1/2.t\geq 3a+b+1/2. The argument for the second case in Part (a) of Theorem 1 shows clearly that 𝒟t,a,b{\mathcal{D}}_{t,a,b} is a closed segment [(xt,yt),(yt,xt)][(x_{t},y_{t}),(y_{t},x_{t})] with xt∈(a,m]x_{t}\in(a,m] for every t≥3​a+b+1/2.t\geq 3a+b+1/2. Besides, the easy fact that

(c,d)∈𝒟a,b⟹(c,d+s)∈𝒟a,b​for every s≥0(c,d)\,\in\,{\mathcal{D}}_{a,b}\;\Longrightarrow\;(c,d+s)\,\in\,{\mathcal{D}}_{a,b}\;\;\mbox{for every $s\geq 0$}

which was used in the argument for the third case in Part (a) of Theorem 1, implies that the function t↦xtt\mapsto x_{t} is non-increasing and that the function t↦ytt\mapsto y_{t} is increasing. Finally, both functions are clearly continuous by the closedness of 𝒟a,b.{\mathcal{D}}_{a,b}. Consider now the mapping

fa,b​(u)={3​a+b+1/2−uif u∈[(3​a+b)/2+1/4,max⁡(2​a+b,a+1/2)]x​(y−1​(u))if u>max⁡(2​a+b,a+1/2),f_{a,b}(u)\;=\;\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}3a+b+1/2-u&\mbox{if $u\in[(3a+b)/2+1/4,\max(2a+b,a+1/2)]$}\\ x(y^{-1}(u))&\mbox{if $u>\max(2a+b,a+1/2),$}\end{array}\right.

which is continuous and non-increasing on [(3a+b)/2+1/4,∞).[(3a+b)/2+1/4,\infty). Putting everything together with Theorem 1 implies the required equivalence (8), and it is clear that (a) is fulfilled. To show (b) and conclude the proof of the Theorem, it suffices to combine (9) and Theorem 4.2 in [5].

□\square

From the above discussion, the latter result can also be expressed in terms of the hypergeometric function F21.{}_{1}F_{2}. More precisely, it follows from (9) that

F21​[.2​ab​c.;−x]≥ 0for all x≥0⟺(b−a,c−a)∈𝒟a,a{}_{1}F_{2}\biggl[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{2a}{b,c};-x\biggr]\;\geq\;0\quad\mbox{for all $x\geq 0$}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;(b-a,c-a)\;\in\;{\mathcal{D}}_{a,a}

for every a,b,c>0.a,b,c>0. This functional representation for the diagram of non-negativity of F21{}_{1}F_{2} on the negative half-line seems unnoticed. Following the introduction in [5], one can also rephrase a problem of Askey and Szegö in the following way : for every a,b>0a,b>0 one has

∫0xtb−a​Ja+b−1​(t)​𝑑t≥ 0for all x≥0⟺(a,1)∈𝒟b,b.\int_{0}^{x}t^{b-a}J_{a+b-1}(t)\,dt\;\geq\;0\quad\mbox{for all $x\geq 0$}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;(a,1)\;\in\;{\mathcal{D}}_{b,b}.

Perhaps can this probabilistic reformulation of an old and celebrated problem on Bessel functions of the first kind - see also Chapter 7.6 in [1] for a discussion - be useful. We would like to finish this paper with the following open problem, which is natural in view of Remark (a).

Conjecture​​ .

For every a,b>0,a,b>0, the set 𝒟a,b{\mathcal{D}}_{a,b} is convex.

This conjecture amounts to the convexity of the function fa,b.f_{a,b}. This would imply that the latter function is also decreasing, in other words that the non-increasing function t↦xtt\mapsto x_{t} which was introduced during the proof of Theorem 2 is actually decreasing. But we were not able to prove this.

Appendix

In this Appendix, we give an independent proof of the classical Weber-Schafheitlin formula, which is the exact computation of a certain Mellin transform. Let us mention that this formula has been given several generalizations over the years - see e.g. [2, 14, 10] and the references therein. The latter, however, do not seem to have direct applications in our setting.

Proposition​​ (Weber-Schafheitlin).

For every α>−1/2\alpha>-1/2 and s∈(0,α+1/2),s\in(0,\alpha+1/2), one has

∫0∞z−2​sJα2(z)dz=Γ⁡(s)​Γ​(α+1/2−s)2​π​Γ​(1/2+s)​Γ​(α+1/2+s)⋅\int_{0}^{\infty}z^{-2s}\,J_{\alpha}^{2}(z)\,dz\;=\;\frac{{\Gamma}(s){\Gamma}(\alpha+1/2-s)}{2\sqrt{\pi}{\Gamma}(1/2+s){\Gamma}(\alpha+1/2+s)}\cdot

The proof relies on the following computation of a Fourier transform, which is originally due to von Lommel. Observe in passing that this simple computation provides a family of solutions to the so-called Van Dantzig problem - see Theorem 1 and Corollary 2 in [8].

Lemma​​ (von Lommel).

For every α>−1/2\alpha>-1/2 and z∈ℂ/ℝ−,z\in{\mathbb{C}}/\penalty{\mathbb{R}}^{-}, one has

1π​Γ​(α+1/2)​(z2)α​∫−11ei​t​z​(1−t2)α−1/2​𝑑t=Jα​(z).\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}\,{\Gamma}(\alpha+1/2)}\,\left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{\alpha}\int_{-1}^{1}e^{{\rm i}tz}(1-t^{2})^{\alpha-1/2}\,dt\;=\;J_{\alpha}(z).
Proof.

Expanding ei​t​ze^{{\rm i}tz} as a series, switching the sum and the integral, cancelling the odd terms and changing the variable, the right-hand side transforms into

1π​Γ​(α+1/2)​(z2)α​∑n≥0(−1)n​z2​n(2​n)!​∫01tn−1/2​(1−t)α−1/2​𝑑t\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}\,{\Gamma}(\alpha+1/2)}\left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{\alpha}\sum_{n\geq 0}(-1)^{n}\frac{z^{2n}}{(2n)!}\,\int_{0}^{1}t^{n-1/2}(1-t)^{\alpha-1/2}\,dt =\displaystyle= (z2)α​∑n≥0(−1)n​Γ⁡(n+1/2)​z2​nπ​(2​n)!​Γ​(n+α+1)\displaystyle\!\left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{\alpha}\,\sum_{n\geq 0}(-1)^{n}\frac{{\Gamma}(n+1/2)\,z^{2n}}{\sqrt{\pi}\,(2n)!\,{\Gamma}(n+\alpha+1)}
=\displaystyle= ∑n≥0(−1)n​(z/2)2​n+αn!​Γ​(n+α+1)=Jα​(z),\displaystyle\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{(-1)^{n}\,(z/2)^{2n+\alpha}}{n!\,{\Gamma}(n+\alpha+1)}\;=\;J_{\alpha}(z),

where the second equality follows from Gauss’ multiplication formula - see e.g. Theorem 1.5.1 in [1].

□\square

We now proceed to our proof of the Proposition. The original argument is the consequence of a more general result involving a quadratic transformation of some hypergeometric function - see [15] p.402 for details and also Exercise 4.15 in [1] for a more modern presentation of this result. We follow here another, apparently unnoticed and overall simpler argument relying on the above Lommel formula, the Fresnel integral and the Selberg integral. For every α>−1/2\alpha>-1/2 and s∈(0,α+1/2),s\in(0,\alpha+1/2), the above Lemma implies first

=\displaystyle= 4α−1/2​Γ​(α+1/2−s)π​Γ​(α+1/2)2​Γ​(s−α)​∫[0,1]2(t⁡(1−t)​u​(1−u))α−1/2​|t−u|2​s−2​α−1​𝑑t​𝑑u\displaystyle\frac{4^{\alpha-1/2}{\Gamma}(\alpha+1/2-s)}{\sqrt{\pi}\,{\Gamma}(\alpha+1/2)^{2}{\Gamma}(s-\alpha)}\int_{[0,1]^{2}}(t(1-t)u(1-u))^{\alpha-1/2}|t-u|^{2s-2\alpha-1}dt\,du
